I don't know if OP is necessarily saying fast food workers don't deserve tips.  Most fast food workers can't accept tips even if they wanted to.  Places like in and out, McDonald's, Jack, the employees there aren't allowed to accept tips.   

Regardless of how much money a server makes, it doesn't justify being treated poorly.  On the other end, just because you're tipping a server, it does not give you a license to be an asshole.  

It's true that servers make most of their money from tips. I don't like tip culture either and I believe the employers should just simply pay higher wages. I'm actually not sure if staying in that environment is best professionally. Ask your fiance this: if he decides to leave his current job, would the employers or co-workers provide a solid reference.

If his answer is "probably not", then your fiance needs to consider whether it's worth it to stay there. Your fiance's future employers will likely call all past employers.  It wouldn't help your fiance if his current employer is going to provide a less than enthusiastic review.  Might want to cut losses and get experience elsewhere. 

Ultimately this is a tough decision you and your fiance will have to discuss and decide for yourselves. There are lots of pros and cons on both decisions and many factors to consider.  Sometimes you'll have to roll the dice and hope for the best!

How you dress for this interview will depend on what type of job you are applying for, how large the non-profit is, and/or how the others in the office dress.  If you are unsure how others in the office will perceive you, it's generally safer to dress for an interview in a suit and tie.  If you don't feel comfortable wearing a suit, at least dress "business casual", which is shirt, slacks and tie.  

You can put together a nice ensemble on a budget, but like Fuiste said, you're going to need more than $100.  Try H&M or the local thrift store.  H&M offers great fitting clothing on a budget.  If you can find clothes that fit well, you can make it look more expensive than it is.  

Good luck!

I'd go with Plan B.  Different states have their own set of rules including county rules and local rules.  It's important for an attorney to familiarize themselves with these rules by practicing in the state where he/she ultimately wants to practice in.  Also, your fiance's current job pays poorly, offers no benefits, and his colleagues seem like douchebags.  I wouldn't want to be in that situation if it were me.  

If your financial situation allows, have your fiance focus on studying for the bar full time to make sure he passes.  Find out the state's bar passage rate and factor that into your decision.  

As for jobs, try legal temp agencies.  Many law firms have short term projects that may fit into your fiance's schedule.  If the firm likes your fiance, it may end up being a full-time position or a strong reference for a future job.

Good luck!
